title: The Fertility Crisis Isn't Just About Who Does the Dishes
gist: Peter Foreshaw Brookes, drawing on IFS's 'Baby Nudges' survey of ~10,000 people in 12 countries, rejects Claudia Goldin's Incomplete Gender Revolution Hypothesis: feeling overburdened by chores shows no negative link to women's fertility intentions. Pro-family values, religiosity and kin orientation predict fertility far better and are weakest in East Asia.

themes.theme: Testing Goldin's Incomplete Gender Revolution Hypothesis

insights.claim: Claudia Goldin's Incomplete Gender Revolution Hypothesis holds that low fertility in rich countries is explained by women bearing a disproportionate share of housework and child care while also working, leading them to rationally opt out of childbearing.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: This hypothesis underpins policy pushes for subsidized child care and male domestic sharing as pronatal levers.
insights.quote: According to Goldin, women are simply rationally opting out of a bad deal.

insights.claim: In a survey of about 10,000 people across 12 countries, there was no significant negative association between feeling overburdened by household chores and any fertility indicator, for men or women, parents or childless, under-35s or couples.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Undercuts the rationale for child-care subsidies and chore-sharing campaigns as effective fertility policy.

insights.claim: The only significant chore effect ran opposite to the hypothesis: partnered men who felt they did more chores than they should were 21.5% less likely to intend another child, while similarly burdened partnered women had a non-significant 1.1% higher chance.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Men's fertility intentions may be more sensitive to perceived domestic unfairness than women's.

insights.claim: Objective measures of specific household tasks also showed essentially no relationship with fertility indicators, and the cross-country correlation between chore burden and fertility intentions was weak and, if anything, positive.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: The null result is robust to perception vs task-based measures and to country-level comparisons.

themes.theme: Values and religiosity drive fertility intentions

insights.claim: Believing that 'children are the future' of the community explains far more variation in intentions to have another child than feeling one does too many chores, and belief that children are the greatest joy also predicts intentions and desired family size.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Pronatal policy may work better through cultural and values channels than through labor-division or child-care spending.

themes.theme: East Asia's values gap explains its ultra-low fertility

insights.claim: Pro-fertility beliefs were at their lowest prevalence in East Asia, with Korean, Japanese and overseas Chinese speakers least likely to value carrying on the family name.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: East Asia's demographic decline (and its consequences for labor supply, consumption and growth) may be resistant to purely economic policy fixes.

insights.claim: Mainland China, Japan, Korea and overseas East Asian Chinese speakers had the lowest religiosity in the 12-country survey and the lowest agreement that people should have as many children as God gives them, while Western respondents were more religious and pro-family.
insights.speaker: Institute for Family Studies
insights.so_what: Values differences, not chore division, may explain the East Asia vs West fertility gap.
